###### Abstract

Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents.
Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement
(RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution
costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving
harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In
this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated
tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests.
Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with
different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate
harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses
normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused
(lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for
different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next
iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our
experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench,
using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these
benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro
achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an
average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage
also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at
[this link](https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro).

## 1 Introduction

An agent harness is the software infrastructure that manages
interactions between a large language model (LLM) and its
environment ([Grace et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). Recent work on recursive
self-improvement (RSI) ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)) uses past
execution trajectories to diagnose problems and guide harness updates
that improve performance on future tasks ([Suzgun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22); [Lin et al., 2026](#bib.bib6); [Pan et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib9)). However, these methods often pursue performance
gains through more extensive exploration and stronger verification ([Lin
et al., 2026](#bib.bib6); [Pan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9)). These efforts
improve performance, but often at the cost of higher token consumption
and increased latency. This trade-off is less appealing in practical
deployment, where the execution cost and latency also matter. We
therefore ask: _Can recursive harness self-improvement deliver better
performance at lower execution cost?_

Toward this goal, we introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for
recursive harness self-improvement that uses both performance and cost
metrics to guide harness updates and candidate selection. It
orchestrates several specialized agents to turn execution feedback into
successive harness updates. A trajectory analyzer examines repeated
rollouts to identify failures and avoidable overhead. Guided by
different performance-cost priorities, a planner turns these diagnoses
into harness improvement plans, which an editor implements as executable
harness candidates. A test-synthesis agent provides fixed tests for
evaluating the candidates without access to ground-truth solutions or
official tests. Candidates that underperform the initial harness or are
Pareto-dominated are discarded. To accommodate different budgets, we
then use normalized weighted squared-distance selection ([Marler and
Arora, 2004](#bib.bib10)) to retain representative harnesses for
cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy)
modes. The selected harnesses then enter the next epoch, where further
updates pursue different performance-cost priorities.

We evaluate HarnessPro on Terminal-Bench 2 ([The Terminal-Bench Team,
2025](#bib.bib19)), SWE-Bench Pro ([Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)), and
ProgramBench ([Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib21)), using GPT-5.5 with
Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. With both backbone models,
HarnessPro improves task performance while reducing execution cost. For
example, on Terminal-Bench 2 with GPT-5.5 and Codex, the heavy mode of
HarnessPro outperforms RHO ([Pan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9)) in pass rate
by 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean cost per task by 33.9%. For
more cost-sensitive deployments, the medium mode delivers performance
comparable to RHO at substantially lower execution cost.

An analysis of the evolved harnesses shows that HarnessPro does not
improve agents simply by compressing context or increasing reasoning
effort. The evolved harnesses dynamically allocate reasoning effort and
tool budgets based on task descriptions, while runtime hooks steer
execution from exploration toward convergence based on the assigned
budgets. They also adopt tool-output compression like RTK ([Szymkowiak,
2026](#bib.bib26)) and streamline instructions to reduce redundant
prompt content, while retaining necessary context and final
verification. Together, these mechanisms curb avoidable overhead while
preserving the reasoning and verification needed for task success,
thereby advancing the performance-cost Pareto frontier. Our
contributions are threefold:

- •
  We introduce HarnessPro, a multi-agent framework that simultaneously
  optimizes performance and cost by analyzing execution trajectories and
  recursively improving harnesses.
- •
  We assess candidate artifacts with fixed LLM-generated tests rather
  than direct LLM judgments, improving failure detection without access
  to official tests.
- •
  Across three benchmarks, HarnessPro improves performance while
  reducing cost and latency, yielding a series of harnesses with
  different performance-cost trade-offs.

## 2 Related Work

##### Agent and harness optimization.

Agent optimization has expanded from prompts and pre-defined workflows
to the executable harness surrounding a model. AFlow searches graphs of
model-invoking operators using execution feedback ([Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5)). More recent systems directly modify harness
components: agentic harness engineering makes edits traceable ([Lin et
al., 2026](#bib.bib6)), HarnessFix diagnoses failures before applying
repairs ([Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib7)), and HarnessX composes
harnesses from typed primitives using trajectory evidence ([Chen et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib8)). RHO uses LLMs to evaluate and compare execution
trajectories without ground-truth labels, guiding harness evolution
toward higher task success ([Pan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9)). In
contrast, our method, HarnessPro, optimizes both task success rate and
monetary cost. Rather than returning a single harness, it produces a set
of harnesses with different performance-cost trade-offs, organized into
lite, medium, and heavy tiers.

##### Component optimization and inference-time budget allocation.

Some methods focus on specific components, such as skills or
memory ([Pan et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11)). SkillOpt optimizes skill
documents ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib12)), while SkillMOO and FRAMES
incorporate cost or regression constraints into skill evolution ([Gong
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib13); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)). Dynamic
Cheatsheet and ReasoningBank retain reusable strategies from past
experience ([Suzgun et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Ouyang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)), while Sleep-time Compute builds reusable memory by
reasoning over context before a query arrives ([Lin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24)). MemoryCPT jointly optimizes memory construction,
retrieval, and summarization ([Lei et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)). Other
work addresses budget allocation at inference time: BATS learns a
budget-aware policy for allocating model tokens and external tool
calls ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)), while COMPAS jointly selects
models, prompts, and decoding settings according to task
difficulty ([Gong et al., 2026b](#bib.bib17)). HarnessPro instead uses
past trajectories to evolve the entire harness, including instructions,
skills, tools, hooks, and verification rules.
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Component optimization and inference-time budget allocation. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")
summarizes how HarnessPro differs from prior work.

| Method                                      | Goal        | Scope          | Feedback     | Iteration    | Output     |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------- | -------------- | ------------ | ------------ | ---------- |
| AFlow ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib5))     | Pass        | Workflow       | Ground truth | Recursive    | Single     |
| SkillMOO ([Gong et al., 2026a](#bib.bib13)) | Pass + Cost | Skills         | Ground truth | Recursive    | Pareto set |
| RHO ([Pan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9))        | Pass        | Skills + tools | Label-free   | Single round | Single     |
| AHE ([Lin et al., 2026](#bib.bib6))         | Pass        | Harness        | Ground truth | Recursive    | Single     |
| HarnessPro                                  | Pass + Cost | Harness        | Label-free   | Recursive    | Pareto set |

Table 1: Comparison of different harness self-improvement methods.

## 3 Problem Setting

A _harness_ $`h\in\mathcal{H}`$ is the software runtime layer that
manages a foundation model’s interactions and execution. It includes
prompts, tools and skills, context and memory mechanisms, hooks, and
verification policies ([Yehudai et al., 2026](#bib.bib1); [OpenAI,
2026](#bib.bib2)). Given a task $`x`$, the harness determines what
information the agent receives, which actions it can take, and how those
actions are executed, directly influencing both task success and
resource consumption. An agent equipped with harness $`h`$ solves task
$`x`$, producing a trajectory $`\tau_{h}(x)=\operatorname{Solve}(h,x)`$
that records tool calls, environment feedback, and the final artifact.
Recursive self-improvement uses trajectories from previous tasks to
guide harness evolution and improve performance on future tasks. Below,
we define the three evaluation metrics: pass rate, execution cost, and
runtime latency.

##### Pass rate.

To prevent test-set leakage, we partition tasks into training,
validation, and test sets, denoted by $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}`$,
$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}`$, and $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}`$.
Outcomes on the training set are used to update harnesses, while the
validation set is used to evaluate and select candidate harnesses. The
test set is used only for final evaluation after evolution. For a task
$`x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}`$, the official tests evaluate the
final artifact produced by $`\tau_{h}(x)`$. We set
$`\operatorname{Pass}(\tau_{h}(x))=1`$ if all official tests pass and
$`\operatorname{Pass}(\tau_{h}(x))=0`$ otherwise. The pass rate is the
fraction of test tasks that pass all official tests,
$`\mathrm{PR}(h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}}\operatorname{Pass}\!\left(\tau_{h}(x)\right)`$.

##### Cost.

We compute execution cost from token usage, distinguishing uncached
input, cached input, and output tokens because they are billed at
different prices. For each task $`x`$, we aggregate these token counts
over all model calls in $`\tau_{h}(x)`$ and compute its cost
$`c_{h}(x)`$ using the prices in
Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Token pricing. ‣ A.2 Additional Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")).
We report the average cost per test task as
$`C(h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}}c_{h}(x)`$.

##### Latency.

We define task latency as the wall-clock time from the start of agent
execution to its completion:
$`\ell_{h}(x)=T_{\mathrm{end}}(\tau_{h}(x))-T_{\mathrm{start}}(\tau_{h}(x))`$.
The time spent grading the final output is not included in task latency.
We average task latencies over the test set to obtain the mean latency,
$`L(h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}}\ell_{h}(x)`$.
Because model response times fluctuate with server load and network
conditions, we treat latency as an auxiliary metric rather than an
optimization objective.

##### Optimization objective.

We aim to evolve harnesses that improve performance while reducing cost.
We formulate the optimization problem as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\left(-\mathrm{PR}(h),\,C(h)\right)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathrm{PR}(h)\geq\mathrm{PR}(h_{0}).
``` |  | (1) |

Here, $`h_{0}`$ is the initial harness. We seek the Pareto frontier and
select three representative operating points: cost-focused (*lite*),
balanced (*medium*), and performance-focused (*heavy*). However, finding
these trade-offs poses two challenges. (1) A vast harness search space.
A harness comprises components such as instructions, tools, skills,
hooks, and rules, all of which can be modified during evolution. Their
possible combinations create a vast, discrete search space that cannot
be optimized using gradients. (2) Balancing performance and cost.
Additional reasoning, exploration, or verification can improve
performance but also consumes more tokens, increasing cost. Conversely,
indiscriminately reducing these activities may hurt performance.
Advancing the Pareto frontier thus requires analyzing execution
trajectories alongside task outcomes and token usage to distinguish
necessary computation from avoidable overhead and find the “sweet spot”
that reduces cost without compromising performance.

## 4 HarnessPro

Figure 1: Overview of HarnessPro. In each epoch, it analyzes rollout
trajectories, generates candidate harnesses, and selects representatives
based on performance and cost.

To address these challenges, we introduce HarnessPro, a multi-agent
framework that analyzes execution trajectories and iteratively modifies
harnesses to advance the performance-cost Pareto frontier. We first
outline the evolution process, then describe trajectory-based diagnosis
and candidate generation, followed by test-based evaluation and
selection.

### 4.1 Overview

To keep trajectory collection and analysis manageable, we begin by
selecting a training coreset $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}`$. Following
RHO ([Pan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9)), we use the Determinantal Point
Process (DPP) kernel ([Kulesza and Taskar, 2012](#bib.bib18)) to balance
task difficulty and diversity
(Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 DPP-Based Coreset Selection ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")).
Starting from an executable harness $`h_{0}`$, we maintain a candidate
set $`\mathcal{A}_{t}`$ of harnesses at epoch $`t`$, initialized as
$`\mathcal{A}_{0}=\{h_{0}\}`$. In each epoch, HarnessPro employs a
multi-agent framework to analyze trajectories of these candidate
harnesses on the coreset $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}`$ to identify
task failures, unproductive exploration, and redundant computation. The
framework then plans and implements harness modifications to address
these issues, producing new executable candidate harnesses as described
in
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Trajectory Analysis and Harness Evolution ‣ 4 HarnessPro ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").

We evolve harnesses in a label-free setting, without access to
ground-truth solutions, official test cases, or graders. Instead of
using an LLM to assess and compare trajectories directly, as in
RHO ([Pan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9)), we use it to generate tests from
task descriptions and trajectories produced by the initial harness. In
each epoch, we evaluate candidate harnesses on the validation set using
the generated tests, measuring pass rate and execution cost. After
discarding candidates that fall below the performance floor or are
Pareto-dominated, we use normalized weighted squared-distance selection
to retain representatives for cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium),
and performance-focused (heavy) modes. The selected harnesses form the
candidate set for the next epoch. This process repeats until the epoch
limit is reached, after which we fix the harnesses and evaluate them on
the test set.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4.1 Overview ‣ 4 HarnessPro ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")
summarizes the full procedure.

$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}},\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}`$; prompts
$`I_{1}`$–$`I_{3}`$; rollouts $`G`$; epoch limit $`T`$

$`h^{T}_{\mathrm{medium}}`$, and heavy $`h^{T}_{\mathrm{heavy}}`$ modes.

$`x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}`$

4:
$`\mathcal{S}(x)\leftarrow\operatorname{\mathbf{TestSynth}}(x,\tau_{h_{0}}(x))`$
for each $`x`$ $`\triangleright`$ Generate once

$`\mathcal{S}`$; fix its initial pass rate
$`\mathrm{PR}_{\mathrm{val}}(h_{0})`$ as the performance floor

### 4.2 Trajectory Analysis and Harness Evolution

At epoch $`t`$, we run each harness in the current candidate set
$`\mathcal{A}_{t}=\{h_{i}^{t}\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{A}_{t}|}`$
independently $`G`$ times on every training task
$`x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}`$. For candidate harness
$`h\in\mathcal{A}_{t}`$, this rollout process yields a trajectory
$`\tau_{h}^{t,g}(x)`$ and a metric vector
$`m_{h}^{t,g}(x)=\left(\operatorname{Pass}_{h}^{t,g}(x),\ c_{h}^{t,g}(x),\ \ell_{h}^{t,g}(x)\right)`$.
Here, $`\operatorname{Pass}_{h}^{t,g}(x)`$ is 1 if the artifact produced
in $`\tau_{h}^{t,g}(x)`$ passes all generated tests in
$`\mathcal{S}(x)`$, while $`c_{h}^{t,g}(x)`$ and $`\ell_{h}^{t,g}(x)`$
record its execution cost and latency. We also retain token usage and
tool-call details for later diagnosis. These trajectories and artifacts
guide harness self-improvement through a multi-agent framework
comprising a trajectory analyzer, an evolution planner, a harness
editor, and a test synthesizer. We describe each agent below.

##### Trajectory Analyzer.

Execution trajectories can reveal harness weaknesses, but the relevant
evidence is often dispersed across long sequences of model responses and
tool outputs, making these weaknesses difficult to locate and interpret.
We therefore implement a trajectory-analysis agent to diagnose these
problems for each candidate $`h`$ and task $`x`$ at epoch $`t`$. To
reduce the impact of randomness, the agent jointly examines the
trajectories $`\{\tau_{h}^{t,g}(x)\}_{g=1}^{G}`$ from $`G`$ independent
rollouts and their metrics $`\{m_{h}^{t,g}(x)\}_{g=1}^{G}`$, rather than
relying on a single attempt:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z(h,x)=\operatorname{Analyzer}\!\left(x,\left\{\left(\tau_{h}^{t,g}(x),m_{h}^{t,g}(x)\right)\right\}_{g=1}^{G}\right).
``` |  | (2) |

The analyzer’s output $`z(h,x)`$ reports (1) identified problems, (2)
their impact on performance and cost, and (3) their sources and
supporting evidence. The evidence includes a concise trajectory summary
or relevant excerpts, together with the path of the trajectory file and
the relevant event range. Two examples are provided in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Trajectory Diagnoses ‣ Appendix C Representative Multi-Agent Artifacts ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").
We combine diagnoses across different tasks as
$`\mathbf{z}(h)=\bigcup\nolimits_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}}z(h,x)`$.
If $`\mathbf{z}(h)`$ exceeds 64K tokens, the analyzer summarizes it. We
similarly collect the metric vectors across training tasks as
$`\mathbf{m}(h)=\bigcup\nolimits_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}}\{m_{h}^{t,g}(x)\}_{g=1}^{G}`$.
The planner uses these diagnoses and metrics to guide its proposals.

##### Evolution Planner.

Building on these diagnoses, the planner proposes three improvement
plans for each candidate. Each plan is guided by a distinct instruction:
$`I_{1}`$ emphasizes cost reduction, $`I_{2}`$ balances performance and
cost, and $`I_{3}`$ prioritizes performance, as detailed in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Evolution Instructions ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").
The planner starts with the full implementation of $`h_{i}^{t}`$, using
its diagnoses and metrics to identify where modifications are needed. It
also compares harness $`h_{i}^{t}`$ and the other candidates
$`h_{k}^{t}`$ by examining their code differences
$`\operatorname{Diff}(h_{i}^{t},h_{k}^{t})`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{p}_{j}(h_{i}^{t})=\operatorname{Plan}(I_{j},h_{i}^{t},\mathbf{z}(h_{i}^{t}),\mathbf{m}(h_{i}^{t}),\{(\operatorname{Diff}(h_{i}^{t},h_{k}^{t}),\mathbf{z}(h_{k}^{t}),\mathbf{m}(h_{k}^{t}))\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq i\end{subarray}}).
``` |  | (3) |

By comparing candidates, the planner can identify effective mechanisms
and remaining bottlenecks. Each plan explains which components to
modify, how to modify them, and the expected effects on performance and
cost, as exemplified in
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Evolution Plans ‣ Appendix C Representative Multi-Agent Artifacts ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").
Full trajectories are not provided to the planner by default. When
needed, it can inspect them using the file paths recorded in the
diagnoses. The planner is instructed to propose generalizable, rather
than task-specific, harness updates. Throughout evolution, the
validation and test sets remain hidden from the planner to avoid
benchmark leakage.

##### Harness Editor.

We then design a harness editor to modify candidate $`h_{i}^{t}`$,
producing a new, executable candidate harness using the proposed plan
$`\mathbf{p}_{j}(h_{i}^{t})`$ and the diagnoses
$`\mathbf{z}(h_{i}^{t})`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{h}_{i,j}^{t}=\operatorname{Edit}\!\left(h_{i}^{t},\mathbf{z}(h_{i}^{t}),\mathbf{p}_{j}(h_{i}^{t})\right),\qquad j=1,2,3.
``` |  | (4) |

Each of the three plans is implemented in a separate workspace, and the
resulting harness is committed to Git so that changes can be traced and
reverted. Newly generated harnesses form $`\mathcal{C}_{t}`$, and we
combine them with the parent harnesses in $`\mathcal{A}_{t}`$ for
evaluation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{C}_{t}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{A}_{t}|}\left\{\widetilde{h}_{i,1}^{t},\widetilde{h}_{i,2}^{t},\widetilde{h}_{i,3}^{t}\right\},\qquad\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{t}=\mathcal{A}_{t}\cup\mathcal{C}_{t}.
``` |  | (5) |

All harnesses in $`\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{t}`$ then undergo the same
evaluation and selection process, as described below.

### 4.3 Evaluation and Candidate Selection

![Refer to caption](2610.26770v2/evaluation_confusion_matrices.png)

Figure 2: Confusion matrices pooled across training tasks from
Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro.

##### Test Synthesizer.

During harness evolution, we follow RHO ([Pan et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib9)), adopting a label-free setting without access to
ground-truth solutions, official tests, or grader feedback. RHO relies
on LLM self-preference to select harnesses. However, we find that LLM
judges tend to be overly optimistic when assessing the execution
trajectories, often treating flawed implementations as successful. We
therefore introduce a dedicated test-synthesis agent to generate test
cases for evaluation; its instruction, skill, and validation tool are
outlined in
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Test Synthesizer Configuration ‣ Appendix C Representative Multi-Agent Artifacts ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").
For each task
$`x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}`$, the
agent generates tests from its description $`x`$ and the initial
trajectory $`\tau_{h_{0}}(x)`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{S}(x)=\operatorname{TestSynth}\!\left(x,\tau_{h_{0}}(x)\right).
``` |  | (6) |

These generated tests remain fixed throughout the self-improvement
process, ensuring a fair comparison among candidate harnesses. A
preliminary experiment demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach,
with failure recall increasing from 41.7% to 83.3% compared with direct
LLM judgments
(Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Evaluation and Candidate Selection ‣ 4 HarnessPro ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")).
After each epoch, we run each candidate
$`h\in\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{t}`$ once per validation task $`x`$ and
check its output against $`\mathcal{S}(x)`$. Task-level pass indicators,
costs, and latencies are averaged to obtain the validation metrics
$`\mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{val}}(h)=\left(\mathrm{PR}_{\mathrm{val}}(h),C_{\mathrm{val}}(h),L_{\mathrm{val}}(h)\right)`$.

##### Candidate filtering and selection.

To prevent the candidate set from growing indefinitely, we retain at
most three harnesses for the next epoch. We first discard candidates
below the initial pass-rate floor $`\mathrm{PR}_{\mathrm{val}}(h_{0})`$
or Pareto-dominated by another candidate:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{t+1}=\left\{h\in\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{t}\ \middle|\ \mathrm{PR}_{\mathrm{val}}(h)\geq\mathrm{PR}_{\mathrm{val}}(h_{0})\;\land\;\not\exists h^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{t}:h^{\prime}\prec h\right\}.
``` |  | (7) |

Figure 3: Schematic of recursive harness update, filtering, and
selection.¹¹ 1 In practice, filtering and selection may retain fewer
than three distinct harnesses, see
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.4 Evolution Dynamics ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").

Here, $`h^{\prime}\prec h`$ denotes Pareto dominance: $`h^{\prime}`$ is
no worse than $`h`$ on both metrics and strictly better on at least one.
We select representatives using a normalized weighted squared-distance
criterion ([Marler and Arora, 2004](#bib.bib10)) that accounts for
actual differences in performance and cost. We first measure each
candidate’s normalized deviations from the highest pass rate and lowest
cost:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{perf}}(h)`$ | $`\displaystyle=(P_{\max}-\mathrm{PR}_{\mathrm{val}}(h))/(P_{\max}-P_{\min}),`$ |  | (8) |
|  | $`\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{cost}}(h)`$ | $`\displaystyle=(C_{\mathrm{val}}(h)-C_{\min})/(C_{\max}-C_{\min}).`$ |  |  |

Here, $`P_{\min},P_{\max}`$ and $`C_{\min},C_{\max}`$ are the extrema of
validation pass rate and mean cost over the current filtered set
$`\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{t+1}`$. The selection objective for mode
$`m`$ is
$`J_{m}(h)=\alpha_{m}d_{\mathrm{perf}}(h)^{2}+\beta_{m}d_{\mathrm{cost}}(h)^{2}`$,
where $`\alpha_{m}`$ and $`\beta_{m}`$ weight performance and cost,
respectively. Each mode
$`m\in\{\mathrm{lite},\mathrm{medium},\mathrm{heavy}\}`$ independently
selects the candidate with the smallest weighted squared distance:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
h_{m}^{t+1}=\operatorname{arg\,min}_{h\in\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{t+1}}J_{m}(h).
``` |  | (9) |

The selected harnesses form $`\mathcal{A}_{t+1}`$ for the next round, as
illustrated in
Figure [1](#footnote1 "footnote 1 ‣ Figure 3 ‣ Candidate filtering and selection. ‣ 4.3 Evaluation and Candidate Selection ‣ 4 HarnessPro ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").
Filtering and selection use only validation metrics, with no access to
test-set results. The final harnesses are evaluated on the held-out test
set $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}`$ only after all rounds of recursive
self-improvement are complete.

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

##### Data and implementation.

We evaluate HarnessPro on Terminal-Bench 2 ([The Terminal-Bench Team,
2025](#bib.bib19)), SWE-Bench Pro ([Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)), and
ProgramBench ([Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib21)), covering terminal
tasks, repository-level issue resolution, and program reconstruction.
Following the dataset splitting protocol of RHO ([Pan et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib9)), we hold out 59, 100, and 100 tasks, respectively,
for testing. From the remaining tasks in each benchmark, we select a
10-task training set $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}`$ using the
DPP-based coreset selection method ([Kulesza and Taskar,
2012](#bib.bib18)) described in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Overview ‣ 4 HarnessPro ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").
The remaining tasks form the validation set. We pair GPT-5.5 with Codex
0.147.0 and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code 2.1.231. Each candidate harness
produces $`G=3`$ rollouts per training task in each epoch. Evolution
runs for three epochs on Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, and four on
ProgramBench, retaining up to three harnesses after each epoch. All
methods use the same data splits and grading settings. Further
implementation details are in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").

##### Baselines.

We compare HarnessPro against several strong harness optimization
methods. The original Codex or Claude Code harness is *Vanilla*, the
starting point for optimization. *Dynamic Cheatsheet* ([Suzgun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)) maintains reusable strategies and code snippets,
*ReasoningBank* ([Ouyang et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)) retrieves strategies
distilled from past trajectories, and *Sleep-time Compute* ([Lin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24)) prepares reusable memory before new tasks.
*RHO* ([Pan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9)) revises harness components
through trajectory analysis and selects candidates using LLM
self-preference. To separate the effects of cost-aware and recursive
optimization, we include two RHO variants. *Balance* changes only RHO’s
optimization instruction, asking for better task performance at lower
cost. *RHO+Iteration* runs *Balance* for the same number of epochs as
HarnessPro. Each subsequent epoch starts from the harness selected in
the preceding epoch by the best-of-$`N`$ procedure of RHO.

##### Evaluation metrics.

On Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, a task passes only if all its
official tests pass. For ProgramBench, we follow its official evaluation
protocol ([Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib21)) and report pass rate as the
macro-average of the fraction of test cases passed for each task. We
also report mean cost $`C(h)`$ and latency $`L(h)`$. For HarnessPro, all
metrics are given as mean $`\pm`$ sample standard deviation over three
runs on Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, and two on ProgramBench. The
token prices used to calculate cost are listed in
Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Token pricing. ‣ A.2 Additional Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")
in the appendix.

Table 2: Performance and efficiency across three benchmarks. P denotes
pass rate (%), while C and T denote mean cost (\$) and execution time
(s). We report mean and standard deviation for HarnessPro. On
ProgramBench, P is the macro-average of the fraction of tests passed per
task.

Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")
compares HarnessPro with several baseline methods across three
benchmarks. With GPT-5.5 and Codex, RHO improves performance over
Vanilla on all three benchmarks, but also increases execution cost. On
SWE-Bench Pro, for example, its mean cost per task rises by 42.6%, from
\$1.88 to \$2.68. In contrast, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves the
highest pass rate across all three benchmarks at lower cost than RHO. On
Terminal-Bench 2, the heavy mode of HarnessPro reaches a mean pass rate
of 80.8% across three runs, 4.5 percentage points above RHO, with 33.9%
lower mean cost. The advantage extends to ProgramBench, where its 69.6%
pass rate exceeds RHO’s 68.8% at 17.8% lower mean cost (\$2.95 vs.
\$3.59). These results show that better task performance need not come
at a higher execution cost. For the medium mode, we retain strong task
performance while reducing cost further. On SWE-Bench Pro, it achieves a
79.0% pass rate compared with RHO’s 80.0%, while reducing the average
cost per task by 53.0%, from \$2.68 to \$1.26. The lite mode lowers cost
further, outperforming Vanilla on all three benchmarks while spending
17.7–57.4% less, making it an economical choice for deployment under
strict budget constraints. Even with comparable iteration budgets,
HarnessPro achieves a better performance–cost trade-off than
RHO+Iteration. Our medium mode matches the performance of RHO+Iteration
on Terminal-Bench 2 at 31.7% lower cost. Moreover, on ProgramBench, our
heavy mode raises pass rate by 1.3 percentage points while lowering mean
cost by 5.8%.

The results with GLM-5.2 and Claude Code follow a similar pattern: the
heavy mode of HarnessPro surpasses RHO on all three benchmarks at lower
cost, while the medium and lite modes outperform Vanilla in pass rate,
often at substantially lower cost. Moreover, although latency is not an
objective, cost optimization yields faster task completion in most
cases. For example, on SWE-Bench Pro, our heavy mode reduces mean
latency from RHO’s 520 to 412 seconds.

### 5.3 Analysis of Evolved Harnesses

To understand how HarnessPro improves the performance-cost trade-off, we
inspect its evolved harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro,
they select an execution profile from each task description. Each
profile specifies a reasoning effort level and a tool-call budget. The
lite, medium, and heavy modes use different rubrics for profile
selection. Runtime hooks enforce the selected budget. For example, on
Terminal-Bench 2, when HarnessPro-Medium selects the standard profile,
the hooks remind the agent to produce parallel tool calls and avoid
redundant checks after 14 tool calls, focus on completing and verifying
the task after 26, and block further calls after 44. The reminders are
appended to tool results, preserving the prompt prefix for cache reuse.
Alongside these dynamic mechanisms, the evolved harnesses also reduce
static context redundancy. On Terminal-Bench 2, for instance,
tool-output compression like RTK ([Szymkowiak, 2026](#bib.bib26)) folds
repeated logs and condenses long outputs, while streamlined developer
instructions reduce redundant input. This combination curbs recurring
prompt overhead and limits the context growth caused by verbose tool
feedback, thereby reducing execution cost and latency. Implementation
details of these harnesses are in
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Terminal-Bench 2 ‣ Appendix D Evolved Harness Artifacts ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").

### 5.4 Evolution Dynamics

Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.4 Evolution Dynamics ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")
tracks test-set performance and cost across epochs. Across all three
benchmarks, HarnessPro advances the performance-cost Pareto frontier
through recursive harness self-improvement. On Terminal-Bench 2, each
round of evolution improves the retained Pareto frontier, yielding
higher pass rates at lower costs. For example, the pass rate of the
heavy mode rises from 74.6% in epoch 1 to a mean of 80.8% in epoch 3,
while mean cost per task falls from \$0.91 to \$0.72. The lite and
medium modes also maintain their pass rates from epoch 2 to 3, while
their mean costs fall from \$0.61 to \$0.43 and from \$0.68 to \$0.56,
respectively. The benefits of additional evolution epochs are
particularly clear on SWE-Bench Pro, where a single run may raise pass
rate at the expense of higher cost. In the medium mode, pass rate rises
from 70.0% in epoch 1 to 77.0% in epoch 2, but mean cost also rises from
\$1.57 to \$1.66. Only in epoch 3 does it improve both metrics, with
pass rate rising to 79.0% and mean cost falling to \$1.26 per task. On
ProgramBench, the fourth epoch likewise lowers costs across all three
modes while maintaining similar pass rates. These patterns highlight an
advantage of recursive self-improvement over single-round evolution.

Table 3: Ablations with GPT-5.5 and Codex. In the RHO variants, *+
dynamic routing* selects reasoning effort from task descriptions, *+
budget hooks* append budget reminders to tool results and *+ low
reasoning effort* fixes effort at low.

Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.5 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")
examines the contributions of main components of HarnessPro. We also
report Cost-of-Pass (CoP) ([Erol et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)), the total
execution cost divided by the number of successful tasks. Removing the
planner reduces performance and increases cost in most experiments. For
example, on SWE-Bench Pro, the pass rate of the medium mode drops from
79.0% to 73.0%, while mean cost rises from \$1.26 to \$1.42 per task.
Removing the test synthesizer has a larger impact, with pass rates
dropping by 3.4–10.0 percentage points across both benchmarks and all
three modes. These performance drops highlight the value of our
multi-agent framework. Beyond these component ablations, we also examine
whether RHO can achieve similar gains by simply adopting individual
strategies from our evolved harnesses. As shown in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.5 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs"),
adding either dynamic routing or budget hooks to RHO reduces cost, but
can also degrade task performance. On SWE-Bench Pro, both variants
reduce cost but achieve lower pass rates than RHO’s 80.0%. Uniformly
using low reasoning effort yields larger cost savings but also
substantially degrades performance. Overall, all three RHO variants are
Pareto-dominated by harnesses evolved by HarnessPro, which achieve
higher pass rates at lower cost.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced HarnessPro, a label-free approach to recursive harness
self-improvement that improves task performance while reducing execution
cost. To this end, it coordinates trajectory diagnosis and harness
modification through a multi-agent framework, with a dedicated planner
proposing update plans and LLM-generated tests guiding candidate
evaluation. Rather than producing a single harness, HarnessPro offers
cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy)
alternatives to meet different deployment budgets. Experiments across
three benchmarks show that HarnessPro can improve task performance while
reducing execution cost, with additional benefits in latency. Further
analysis attributes these gains to the synergy of multiple evolved
mechanisms and shows sustained progress through recursive
self-improvement. These findings show that performance and efficiency
can improve together, making cost-aware evolution a promising direction
for practical recursive self-improvement in harness optimization.

#### AI Use Statement

Generative AI tools were used to assist with software implementation and
the drafting and editing of this manuscript. Separately, LLMs are
integral to the method studied in this work: they analyze execution
trajectories, propose and implement harness updates, and synthesize
tests during harness evolution. All AI-assisted code and text were
manually reviewed, and all reported results were checked by the authors.

#### Reproducibility Statement

The full evolution procedure and optimization objective are described in
Sections [3](#S3 "3 Problem Setting ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")
and [4](#S4 "4 HarnessPro ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs"),
with pseudocode in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4.1 Overview ‣ 4 HarnessPro ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs").
Section [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")
specifies the benchmarks, model and agent versions, rollout counts,
evolution epochs, selection hyperparameters, and evaluation metrics. The
appendix provides the evolution instructions, token-pricing assumptions,
and representative artifacts from the frozen evolved harnesses.

## Appendix A Implementation Details

### A.1 DPP-Based Coreset Selection

We select the training coreset once, before harness evolution. Following
RHO ([Pan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9)), let $`\mathcal{U}=\{1,\ldots,M\}`$
index the candidate tasks. For each task $`x_{i}`$, we collect a
trajectory under the initial harness. A language-model judge reads the
task description and trajectory, then assigns a difficulty score
$`r_{i}\in[0,10]`$ and an abstract failure-mode fingerprint
$`\phi_{i}`$. The fingerprint omits task-specific names so that
similarity reflects shared challenges rather than superficial project
details.

Let $`u_{i}`$ be the unit-normalized embedding of $`\phi_{i}`$. We
compute cosine similarity and construct a difficulty-weighted DPP
kernel:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle S_{ij}`$ | $`\displaystyle=u_{i}^{\top}u_{j},\qquad q_{i}=\max(r_{i}/10,\varepsilon),`$ |  | (10) |
|  | $`\displaystyle w_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left(q_{i}/\max_{j}q_{j}\right)^{\alpha},\qquad\alpha=\frac{\theta}{2(1-\theta)},`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle K`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{diag}(w)\,S\,\operatorname{diag}(w).`$ |  |  |

We use $`\varepsilon=0.1`$ and $`\theta=0.7`$, as in RHO. The difficulty
weights favor challenging tasks, while the determinant of a subset’s
kernel penalizes redundant fingerprints. For a fixed coreset size $`k`$,
the corresponding $`k`$-DPP assigns each $`k`$-element subset
$`Y\subseteq\mathcal{U}`$ probability ([Kulesza and Taskar,
2012](#bib.bib18))

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr_{k}(Y)=\frac{\det(K_{Y})}{\sum_{Z\subseteq\mathcal{U},\,|Z|=k}\det(K_{Z})},
``` |  | (11) |

where $`K_{Y}`$ is the principal submatrix indexed by $`Y`$. We do not
sample from this distribution. Instead, we approximate its most probable
subset by greedily adding the task that maximizes the resulting
determinant:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle i_{s}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\arg\max_{i\in\mathcal{U}\setminus Y_{s}}\det(K_{Y_{s}\cup\{i\}}),`$ |  | (12) |
|  | $`\displaystyle Y_{s+1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=Y_{s}\cup\{i_{s}\},\qquad Y_{0}=\emptyset.`$ |  |  |

We stop after $`k=10`$ tasks and keep this coreset fixed across all
evolution epochs. Neither official test results nor validation outcomes
enter coreset selection.

### A.2 Additional Implementation Details

##### Reasoning effort and mode weights.

The default reasoning effort for GPT-5.5 is high on all three
benchmarks. For GLM-5.2, the default is max on Terminal-Bench 2 and
SWE-Bench Pro, but high on ProgramBench, where max tends to induce
extensive reasoning and tool use, substantially lengthening execution.
For the selection rule in
Equation [9](#S4.E9 "In Candidate filtering and selection. ‣ 4.3 Evaluation and Candidate Selection ‣ 4 HarnessPro ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs"),
the performance-cost weights $`(\alpha_{m},\beta_{m})`$ are $`(1,2)`$
for lite, $`(1,1)`$ for medium, and $`(2,1)`$ for heavy. These weights
remain fixed across epochs.

##### Generation settings.

Our Codex configurations use the Responses API without explicitly
setting temperature, top_p, or max_output_tokens. When used through
Codex, GPT-5.5 therefore uses its default sampling settings. The model
supports up to 128,000 output tokens per response.²² 2
[https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.5](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.5)
For GLM-5.2, Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro use temperature 1.0,
top-p 0.95, and a per-request max_tokens of 131,072. On ProgramBench,
GLM-5.2 runtime uses temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0, and max_tokens of
32,000, with a 2,000-turn limit.

##### Solver and grading budgets.

On Terminal-Bench 2, GPT-5.5 uses each task’s native solver limit
(600–3,600 seconds on the test set). On SWE-Bench Pro, the solver time
limit is 1200 seconds for GPT-5.5 and 7,200 for GLM-5.2, and the grader
limit is 3,600 seconds for both models. On ProgramBench, the solver
budget is 7,200 seconds, separate from the 14,400 second outer limit for
each grading branch. These wall-clock limits are distinct from
harness-level tool-call budgets.

##### Task environments.

Terminal-Bench 2 and ProgramBench allocate 8 CPUs and 32 GiB of memory
per solver. SWE-Bench Pro runs solvers in host workspaces without an
explicit per-task CPU or memory limit. Candidate evaluation uses one
rollout per validation task, and final testing is performed only after
evolution. Infrastructure failures are excluded and retried to avoid
inaccurate results.

##### Token pricing.

Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Token pricing. ‣ A.2 Additional Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs")
reports the public API prices used to convert token usage into execution
cost. We use the short-context price tier for GPT-5.5 because all
requests remain below 272K context tokens. Prices follow the official
OpenAI³³ 3
[https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing)
and Z.ai⁴⁴ 4
[https://docs.z.ai/guides/overview/pricing](https://docs.z.ai/guides/overview/pricing)
pricing pages.

| Model                       | Uncached input | Cached input | Output     |
|-----------------------------|----------------|--------------|------------|
| GPT-5.5 ($`<272`$K context) | 5.00 \$/M      | 0.50 \$/M    | 30.00 \$/M |
| GLM-5.2                     | 1.40 \$/M      | 0.26 \$/M    | 4.40 \$/M  |

Table 4: Token prices used to compute execution costs.

## Appendix B Evolution Instructions

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Prioritize reducing average execution cost while preserving task
correctness and

reliable completion. Seek genuine efficiency gains, not lower bills
obtained by

skipping required work, abandoning difficult tasks, or weakening
validation.

Use the diagnostics, trajectories, and candidate implementations to
distinguish

necessary work from avoidable expense. Look for recurring sources of
redundant

exploration, repeated context, or low-value verification. Consider the
total cost of

execution, including unsuccessful attempts and any overhead introduced
by the proposed

change; fewer steps or shorter outputs alone do not establish an
improvement.

Possible directions include adapting reasoning effort to individual
public tasks,

managing context and tool feedback economically, and improving
convergence or recovery.

Preserve the information and checks needed for dependable results. These
are optional

search directions, not a checklist: derive any mechanism from the
available evidence,

without assuming a routing rubric, fixed thresholds, profile taxonomy,
or per-task rules.

Propose a focused, generalizable plan rather than accumulating
optimizations. Explain

which observed expense each change addresses, why correctness should be
preserved,

and what regression risks remain. Distinguish expected savings from
measured results;

the fixed external evaluator, not the plan’s claims, determines whether
quality is

rather than

recoverable

together. Make uncertain trade-offs and regression risks explicit,

## Appendix C Representative Multi-Agent Artifacts

### C.1 Trajectory Diagnoses

These lightly edited analyzer outputs retain issue-level findings from
three rollouts of each Terminal-Bench 2 training task. Outcomes use
fixed LLM-generated tests.

##### Caffe–CIFAR-10.

All three runs failed before training. The analyzer separates a shared
build bottleneck from run-specific stalls and a potential downstream
risk.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Task: Build CPU-only Caffe and train CIFAR-10 for 500 iterations.

Outcome: No run completed conversion or training, saved a model or log,

or verified accuracy.

Issue 1: All three workflows ended before training.

Problem: Run 0 was fixing a protobuf build issue; run 1 had built

Caffe but was downloading CIFAR-10; run 2 was still rebuilding after

an out-of-memory (OOM) failure.

Cost impact: Long installs, builds, and downloads produced no final

training artifacts.

Evidence: run-0-trace-0.jsonl:89-97; run-1-trace-0.jsonl:96-111;

run-2-trace-0.jsonl:74-80.

Issue 2: High build parallelism caused OOM failures in every run.

Problem: Runs 0 and 1 used make all -j\$(nproc), and run 2 used

cmake –build build –parallel 7. OOM-killed compiler processes

prompted lower-parallelism retries.

Quality impact: Runs 0 and 2 still lacked a successful build at the

trace end, delaying data preparation and training.

Cost impact: Failed compile passes and rebuilds wasted time.

Evidence: run-0-trace-0.jsonl:71-89; run-1-trace-0.jsonl:90-96;

run-2-trace-0.jsonl:61-80.

Issue 3: The most advanced run stalled on the CIFAR-10 download.

Problem: Run 1 interrupted a slow single-stream download, installed

aria2, and ended while its replacement parallel download was ongoing.

Quality impact: Conversion, mean generation, training, and model

verification were not reached despite a completed Caffe build.

Cost impact: The interrupted download, package install, and retry

added post-build time without completing data preparation.

Evidence: run-1-trace-0.jsonl:96-111.

Issue 4: A likely downstream data-preparation blocker (not observed).

Problem: Run 0 configured Caffe without OpenCV, although the stock

CIFAR pipeline calls compute_image_mean, which requires USE_OPENCV.

Quality impact: Had run 0 reached this step, mean generation would

likely have failed; the trace does not show such a failure.

Cost impact: An OpenCV-enabled rebuild or alternative preparation path

would likely have been needed after the existing build work.

Evidence: run-0-trace-0.jsonl:60-69; run-1-trace-0.jsonl:69;

run-2-trace-0.jsonl:36-37.

Issue 5: Run 0 recovered from an incorrect source tag.

It tried the nonexistent 1.0.0 branch, inspected tags, then used 1.0;

this added commands before the build but no lasting quality loss.

Evidence: run-0-trace-0.jsonl:27-42.

##### Mailman.

In contrast, all three Postfix/Mailman 3 configurations passed the
generated tests. The diagnosis separates useful end-to-end verification
from broad exploration, redundant checks, and two run-specific detours
that increased cost without changing the final outcome.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Task: Configure a mailing list with join, leave, and post delivery.

Outcome: All three rollouts passed the generated tests.

Issue 1: Exploration went well beyond the relevant configuration.

Problem: All runs dumped large Mailman/Postfix configs and package

source/tests after the task and eval narrowed the relevant surface

to mailman.cfg, Postfix local delivery, and Mailman LMTP maps.

Quality impact: Some inspection helped, but the broader search added

little evidence for final correctness.

Cost impact: Trace totals reached 1,058,946, 1,763,487, and

2,517,861 input tokens in runs 0, 1, and 2, respectively; broad

dumps and repeated exploration were major contributors.

Evidence: run-0-trace-0.jsonl:36-69,86-93,180;

run-1-trace-0.jsonl:22-27,175; run-2-trace-0.jsonl:18-19,180.

Issue 2: Final evaluations repeated already covered behavior.

Problem: Manual join/post/leave smoke tests usefully checked delivery

and leave confirmation, but /app/eval.py was rerun after these and

earlier evaluations had passed.

Quality impact: Extra evals added little end-to-end coverage.

Cost impact: Each eval created Unix users, exercised mail queues,

and included retry sleeps.

Evidence: run-0-trace-0.jsonl:149-153;

run-1-trace-0.jsonl:158-173;

run-2-trace-0.jsonl:102-122,167-170.

Issue 3: Run 2’s smoke test temporarily broke mail delivery.

Problem: Opening /var/mail/\<user\> with mailbox.mbox() before Postfix

created it produced a root-owned mailbox, so confirmation mail bounced.

Quality impact: The agent diagnosed this test-induced failure and

reran the smoke test successfully; the final outcome was unaffected.

Cost impact: Log/queue inspection, qfile decoding, reconnects, and

another full smoke test followed.

Evidence: run-2-trace-0.jsonl:123-152.

Issue 4: A service-control pipeline hung in run 1.

Problem: A daemonized Mailman start inherited a pipe to sed, leaving

the wrapper running after the services started.

Quality impact: Services ran, so the final result was unaffected.

Cost impact: The agent polled, inspected logs and processes, then

terminated the wrapper before evaluation.

Evidence: run-1-trace-0.jsonl:104-126.

Issue 5: A broad recipient-validation workaround carried a risk.

Problem: Run 1 disabled SMTP-time local recipient validation after

lookup failures; run 2 also ended with local_recipient_maps empty.

Quality impact: Delivery passed for valid Unix users. Invalid local

recipients might be accepted at SMTP time and fail later, a risk

not observed in the tests.

Cost impact: Two failed evals and map debugging preceded the fallback.

Evidence: run-1-trace-0.jsonl:130-159;

run-2-trace-0.jsonl:99-100,172-173.

### C.3 Test Synthesizer Configuration

Our test-synthesis agent uses an instruction and skill together with an
MCP-based validation tool. The first two listings present selected
passages from the deployed text, with output-schema fields condensed;
the third summarizes the tool interface. Together, they show how the
agent designs tests from public evidence, checks them against a frozen
artifact, and reviews the suite without access to official tests or
labels.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Use \$empty-test-authoring. In this one Codex invocation, write ten
distinct

executable cases, validate them on the frozen Empty product, inspect the
results,

and self-review the final suite. No separate reviewer is part of this
run.

\## Evidence boundary

Read /work/public-task.json, relevant /public_inputs, and the read-only

/empty_product. The task description and public files define the
contract;

Empty is only an implementation and execution-diagnostic context, never
an

answer key. Public sample programs and evaluation helpers may be used.

…

Do not seek or use the target’s hidden official tests, grader, solution,

grades, or earlier target suites, locally or online. Do not modify
Empty.

\## Test design

Inventory the public requirements and the actual input and output
interfaces

before testing Empty. Cover distinct documented behaviors, valid
alternatives,

boundaries, and justified combinations; do not invent extra obligations
to

fill the fixed count.

…

For each central requirement, invoke the real delivered product and
assert a

meaningful relation between its output and independent public evidence.

A file existing, successful process, shape, nonempty value, or plausible
range

alone does not establish the required behavior.

…

Choose the strongest justified oracle available: compatible public
reference,

known answer, necessary content property, or discriminating metamorphic

relation. Never derive expected constants, hashes, tolerated values, or

execution paths from Empty.

\## Execute and self-review

Write the complete suite, then call validate_generated_tests on it. A
tool

result with status=ok, passed=false is a valid execution with possible
product

failures; making Empty pass is not the objective. infra_error is
inconclusive:

inspect the traceback and public evidence to distinguish test/setup
defects

from product exceptions under valid invocation. Repair only demonstrated
test

defects, preserving the public requirement and legitimate Empty
failures. Do

not skip cases, catch all exceptions, or tune expectations toward Empty.

After every executable edit, rerun the tool; the final executable files
must

match a completed execution without infrastructure error. Run tests
serially.

Self-review every case, expected value, and shared helper after the
final run.

…

\## Output contract

Write UTF-8 files under /work/output, at most 1 MiB per file and 4 MiB
total:

\- test_generated.py: exactly test_case_0001 through test_case_0010 as

unittest.TestCase methods; no skipped or unconditional padding cases.

\- case_manifest.json: expected_count: 10; each case has a meaningful

description and kind behavioral, format, or unavailable_oracle.

\- coverage.json: public evidence, requirements mapped to case IDs,
checks

performed, what was not checked, and limitations.

\- repair-log.json: demonstrated defects, public evidence, edits, and
rerun

outcomes; use \[\] if no repair was needed.

\- self-review.json: per-case assessment, reason, public evidence,
suggested

repair, and any essential or supplemental coverage gaps.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Read /work/public-task.json and relevant /public_inputs first. Inspect

/empty_product only to understand the frozen candidate’s interfaces or
to

diagnose execution. Its files correspond to original paths such as /app,
but

the snapshot is not an oracle. The available public dependencies and
fixture

mounts are listed in validation_environment in the task JSON. Disjoint

examples are read-only under /examples.

Write the suite in /work/output. Invoke the frozen_empty MCP tool

validate_generated_tests after writing executable tests and after each
edit;

the tool executes the current suite in a fresh Empty container and
returns

only synthetic diagnostics. If MCP discovery fails, send a JSON-RPC
tools/call

request to python3 /opt/harnesspro/empty-tools/tools/mcp_server.py on
stdin.

Keep tests and validation calls serial. The model has no Docker socket
or

official grader.

Interpret status=ok, passed=false as a completed execution, not a
request

to make Empty pass. Treat infra_error as unresolved until its cause is

identified. Repair only test defects supported by public evidence,
record

the change in repair-log.json, and rerun the changed suite. Preserve
valid

product failures and report any unresolved oracle or setup problem.
Review

the final test design in the same invocation; do not launch another
reviewer.

Public reference tools, if needed, are available in the authoring image;

version manifests are under /opt/harnesspro/reference-tools. Check that
a

reference is compatible with the public runtime before using exact
outputs.

The main instruction defines the ten-case output and review schema.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Tool: frozen_empty.validate_generated_tests

MCP discovery: tools/list advertises validate_generated_tests

Arguments: {} (no task-specific parameters; extra properties rejected)

Input: the current test suite in /work/output

Request: a validate_generated_tests operation sent through
/empty-tool-rpc

Execution: a fresh container with the frozen Empty product

Response: JSON diagnostics from the suite execution, not official tests,

grader feedback, or labels

Completed execution: status == ok, whether passed is true or false

Infrastructure failure: status == infra_error; MCP isError is true

Timeout: 7,200 seconds; an absent response raises an error rather than

inventing a validation result

#### D.1.1 Medium Mode

The medium mode uses GPT-5.5 throughout, with five execution profiles
spanning low, medium, and high reasoning effort. The listings below
present its instructions, routing rubric, runtime hooks, and policy
settings.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are Codex, a non-interactive software agent. Work autonomously until
the

user’s task is complete. Follow the task’s integrity, safety, path, and
output

requirements exactly. Use the available tools to inspect, edit, execute,
and

verify; batch independent checks and avoid repeating unchanged reads.
Preserve

unrelated files and avoid destructive operations outside the requested
scope.

Do not replace a requested implementation or service with a mock, proxy,
or

look-alike unless the task explicitly permits that substitution.

Do not spawn other agents or ask the user to perform routine steps. Keep

progress messages brief. Before finishing, leave every requested
artifact at

its exact path and run the strongest allowed task-shaped verification.
Report

the outcome concisely, including any genuine remaining uncertainty.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Harness guidance is already loaded; do not inventory harness/. Extract
exact artifacts, paths, behavior, integrity restrictions, public
interfaces, and final state from task/prompt.md. Use its
host-to-container pattern. For black-box work use only public interfaces
and implement general behavior. When the task names an API, wrapper,
package, revision, runtime, or service, exercise that named interface
first and do not silently replace it with a lower-level dependency,
mock, proxy, or look-alike behavior; inspect the public signature or
implementation after an interface error. A source-only or
single-artifact deliverable should not acquire undeclared runtime
helpers. Start with the smallest discriminating probe and batch
independent checks. Bound downloads, external interaction, and
potentially blocking commands well below the task watchdog; reserve time
for final repair and verification. Validate requested behavior, not only
superficial readiness signals. Run mutating workflow checks on
disposable fixtures when possible; if the user is meant to perform the
same workflow later, do not leave test data or state that collides with
its documented preconditions. Preserve the real requested implementation
and durable service state while removing only temporary verification
artifacts. For quantitative work, identify units, variables, invariants,
and the comparison objective before optimizing; exercise every publicly
stated correctness dimension using a direct reference or invariant when
one can be constructed. Keep temporary verification artifacts separate
from final deliverables. Before finishing, compare exact contents and
state with every explicit requirement. Avoid narration and unchanged
rereads; do not skip necessary validation.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Choose exactly one profile from observable task characteristics.
Optimize

expected success per dollar. Never use historical outcomes remembered
from prior

runs or evaluations.

Profiles:

\- ‘compact’: low reasoning; converge near 4 tool calls and stop near 8.

\- ‘lean’: low reasoning; converge near 10 calls and stop near 16.

\- ‘standard’: medium reasoning; converge near 26 calls and stop near
38.

\- ‘deep’: high reasoning; converge near 30 calls and stop near 48.

\- ‘research’: high reasoning with about 40 calls for source
reconstruction.

Evidence rules

\- Use only validation, interaction, dependencies, artifacts, and
constraints

explicitly described in the task text. Never assume hidden-test
behavior,

previous attempts, tool output, runtime results, or historical scores.

\- An undescribed validator has unknown quality, not weak quality.
Unknown decisive

evidence defaults to ‘standard’; missing information alone cannot
justify

another profile.

\- A strong oracle must be explicitly local and repeatable and provide
localized

failure, quantitative error, candidate ranking, deterministic
simulation, or a

directly inspectable target. Compilation, launch, an open port, one
end-to-end

request, or whole-task pass/fail is weak only when the text explicitly
limits

feedback to that undifferentiated signal.

\- Count distinct evidence-resolvable hypotheses, not files, prose,
commands, or

retries. Extra iterations are valuable only when described probes can

distinguish hypotheses and change the plan.

\- Include the stated watchdog and expected probe cost in the value of

iteration. A precise oracle is not useful enough for ‘deep’ when only a
few

full evaluations can fit and high reasoning does not create more
evidence.

Apply the following gates in order and stop at the first match.

Gate 1: ‘compact’

Choose ‘compact’ only when low marginal value is explicit and no
faithful

decomposable oracle is described or structurally possible:

1. Long serial graphical, remote, virtualized, or manual interaction
whose

correctness depends on visual or hidden state.

2. Unavailable accounts, devices, services, credentials, or changing
external

state without a faithful local substitute.

3. Broad hidden or effectively unbounded behavior plus exact
preservation of

unrelated details, with explicitly end-to-end accept/reject feedback.

4. One unchanged artifact must satisfy independent grammars, parsers,
runtimes,

or environments, while checks expose only a joint accept/reject
objective.

5. Bulk media or visual interpretation with no described numerical
comparator

and correctness resting on visual judgment.

Difficulty, visualization, specialization, or virtualization alone is
not enough.

A small fixed visual artifact, scripted headless setup with direct
checks, or

local scorer that distinguishes candidates should continue to later
gates.

File-existence or format checks do not make long visual/media search a
strong

oracle when the decisive event must still be found by inspecting many
frames.

Gate 2: ‘research’

Choose ‘research’ only when the primary deliverable is factual
reconstruction

requiring multiple accessible sources, version/date alignment,
provenance, or a

historical snapshot. A multi-record date/version ranking qualifies; one
lookup or

research used only to build an artifact does not. If decisive sources
are

explicitly inaccessible, choose ‘compact’.

Gate 3: ‘deep’

Choose ‘deep’ only when a strong local oracle is explicitly described or
can be

constructed from an exact deterministic reference, transformation,
simulator, or

runtime supplied by the task, and at least one shape applies:

1. Latent structure or parameter recovery plus exact compatibility or a

quantitative objective.

2. Correctness spans several interacting components, stages, or states
and can be

checked through exact invariants, reference behavior, or round trips.

3. Damaged structured-state recovery requiring competing format,
ordering, or

transformation hypotheses.

4. Constrained synthesis, compression, size reduction, or candidate
search with

coupled hard constraints and an executable scorer.

5. Nontrivial recovery, inference, or attack derived from many
observations with

exact candidate validation.

6. An inverse problem with a deterministic simulator or quantitative
objective.

7. Candidate construction against a deterministic transformation or
runtime,

with multiple materially different mechanisms that can be executed and
observed.

8. A severely constrained reimplementation of deterministic reference
behavior,

where exact candidate outputs can be compared locally despite language,
size,

compatibility, or dependency restrictions.

9. One source artifact must implement behavior while remaining valid
under two

or more independent grammars, compilers, or runtimes, each of which can
be

exercised separately for localized feedback.

Do not choose ‘deep’ for terminology, long specifications, ordinary
security or

reverse engineering, or hidden tests alone. Ordinary performance tuning
and

ordinary state propagation through services, hooks, or deployments are

‘standard’. A binary validator alone is insufficient, but a
deterministic local

transformation plus executable behavior can support meaningful candidate

iteration even when the final verdict is binary. Prefer ‘standard’ when
each

candidate evaluation is described as expensive enough to consume a
material

part of the watchdog and the work is mainly bounded tuning against one
supplied

evaluator. Modifying an existing artifact against one supplied evaluator
remains

‘standard’ merely because it combines a quantitative objective with
preservation

constraints; ‘deep’ additionally requires latent recovery, combinatorial
search,

or several materially different candidate mechanisms. ‘deep’ requires
room for

several evidence-changing iterations.

Gate 4: ‘lean’

Choose ‘lean’ only when all are explicit:

1. Bounded, mostly deterministic work.

2. At most two meaningful uncertainties.

3. A credible plan before broad exploration.

4. A direct local check covering nearly all decisive behavior.

5. About eight or fewer evidence-producing calls for inspection,
implementation,

and final validation.

Typical cases are a localized transformation; enumerable mechanical
cleanup with

a deterministic final scan; a simple build or single-service setup with
one main

uncertainty and a direct test; or bounded numerical work with direct
value, shape,

or residual validation.

Do not choose ‘lean’ when several coupled uncertainties require
iterative

candidate comparison, or when recovering latent state requires
materially

different hypotheses. Apply the ‘deep’ gate first when a constructible
exact or

quantitative reference makes those iterations useful. Also do not choose
‘lean’

for broad cleanup where unaffected content must be preserved exactly and
the

set of true matches is not explicitly bounded; false-positive scope is a

separate uncertainty even when a final scan is deterministic.

Use ‘standard’ when coordinating several schemas, formats, subsystems,

integration boundaries, correctness/performance constraints, or hidden
edge-case

families. Also use it for multi-service state propagation, broad
security

properties, builds combining source provenance with feature exclusion
and

multiple runtime modes, corpus-wide cleanup with exact preservation of
unaffected

content, or unstructured recovery with several evidence paths but only
final

candidate checks.

Gate 5: ‘standard’

Choose ‘standard’ for everything else, including unknown oracle quality.
It is

the default for ordinary implementation, debugging, data processing,
service

setup, bounded numerical work, and analysis with several actionable

uncertainties, and should normally be the plurality.

def \_stage_context(count: int, selection: dict\[str, Any\]) -\> str:

economy = int(selection.get(”economy_after_tools”) or 0)

strict = int(selection.get(”strict_after_tools”) or 0)

reminder = int(selection.get(”strict_reminder_every”) or 8)

if count == economy:

return (

”Economy phase starts now. Batch independent ls/rg/read/test checks,
suppress ”

”process narration, and do not repeat unchanged checks. Do not trade
away the ”

”behavioral validation or exact final-state checks required by the
task.”

)

if count \>= strict and (count == strict or (count - strict) % reminder
== 0):

return (

”Convergence phase: stop broad exploration. Only inspect evidence
directly tied to the ”

”current failure or deliverable. If a concrete failure, unexplained
instability, or ”

”mutated deliverable remains, repair it rather than finalizing because
the phase changed. ”

”Avoid irreversible cleanup or broad state changes not required by the
task, and keep ”

”temporary verification artifacts separate from final deliverables. ”

”Then recheck exact paths, interfaces, behavior, and final state once
and finish.”

)

return ””

def \_compact_text(text: str, \*, head_chars: int, tail_chars: int) -\>
str:

lines = text.splitlines()

deduped: list\[str\] = \[\]

index = 0

while index \< len(lines):

next_index = index + 1

while next_index \< len(lines) and lines\[next_index\] ==
lines\[index\]:

next_index += 1

repeats = next_index - index

deduped.append(lines\[index\])

if repeats \> 2:

deduped.append(f”\[previous line repeated {repeats - 1} more times\]”)

elif repeats == 2:

deduped.append(lines\[index\])

index = next_index

compact = ”\\n”.join(deduped)

if len(compact) \<= head_chars + tail_chars:

return compact

omitted = len(compact) - head_chars - tail_chars

return (

compact\[:head_chars\]

 + f”\\n… \[{omitted} characters omitted; use the raw path for a
targeted range\] …\\n”

 + compact\[-tail_chars:\]

)

Harness guidance is already loaded; do not inventory harness/. Extract
exact artifacts, paths, behavior, integrity restrictions, public
interfaces, and final state from task/prompt.md. Use its
host-to-container pattern. For black-box work use only public interfaces
and implement general behavior. When the task names an API, wrapper,
package, revision, runtime, or service, exercise that named interface
first and do not silently replace it with a lower-level dependency,
mock, proxy, or look-alike behavior; inspect the public signature or
implementation after an interface error. A source-only or
single-artifact deliverable should not acquire undeclared runtime
helpers. Start with the smallest discriminating probe and batch
independent checks. Bound downloads, external interaction, and
potentially blocking commands well below the task watchdog; reserve time
for final repair and verification. Validate requested behavior, not only
superficial readiness signals. For multi-stage services and persistent
state, test from a fresh external entry point and check
repeated-operation behavior, defaults, permissions, and final ownership
instead of trusting internal readiness. For numerical, transformation,
or recovery work, validate against an independent reference, invariant,
round trip, or residual rather than only reusing the implementation’s
own assumptions. Run mutating workflow checks on disposable fixtures
when possible; if the user is meant to perform the same workflow later,
do not leave test data or state that collides with its documented
preconditions. Preserve the real requested implementation and durable
service state while removing only temporary verification artifacts. Keep
temporary verification artifacts separate from final deliverables.
Before finishing, reread the public task once, inspect the actual final
artifact or durable state, and compare every explicit requirement
against independent evidence. Avoid narration and unchanged rereads; do
not skip necessary validation.

### D.2 SWE-Bench Pro

The medium mode harness uses GPT-5.5 and Codex. A separate GPT-5.5 call
uses the rubric to select one of five reasoning and tool-budget profiles
from the public task description. The repository-repair workflow first
extracts the contract, then checks the implementation and available
references, makes a focused patch, and verifies task-shaped behavior.
Listing  shows the stored harness files. The evaluator configures Codex
to load the instructions and register the hook. The repair-verify script
provides basic code checks, while a checklist guides task-specific
verification.

You are Codex, a non-interactive software agent. Work autonomously until
the

user’s task is complete. Follow the task’s integrity, safety, path, and
output

requirements exactly. Use the available tools to inspect, edit, execute,
and

verify; batch independent checks and avoid repeating unchanged reads.
Preserve

unrelated files and avoid destructive operations outside the requested
scope.

Do not replace a requested implementation or service with a mock, proxy,
or

look-alike unless the task explicitly permits that substitution.

Do not spawn other agents or ask the user to perform routine steps. Keep

progress messages brief. Before finishing, leave every requested
artifact at

its exact path and run the strongest allowed task-shaped verification.
Report

the outcome concisely, including any genuine remaining uncertainty.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

The repair workflow is already loaded; do not spend tool calls
inventorying harness/. First establish the repository root under task/
and keep later commands rooted there. Read task/prompt.md as a contract
and keep a concise ledger of exact public names, files, payloads,
defaults, error behavior, compatibility requirements, and stated edge
cases. Inspect the local implementation and nearby tests first. Look for
an existing reference when the task sounds like a known fix: local Git
history, tags, upstream commits, tests, fixtures, or nearby
implementation patterns. Prefer adapting proven behavior over guessing.
Trace the real execution and data path before editing, then make the
smallest production-source change that satisfies the contract. Start
with narrow discriminating probes, batch independent reads and searches,
and avoid unchanged rereads. Reserve enough budget for a post-change
task-shaped test, investigation of any concrete failure, and one final
diff/contract review; compilation alone is insufficient. Use
harness/bin/repair-verify only when its general checks are useful. Keep
generated files, caches, and temporary tests out of the final patch.
Before finishing, inspect the diff and re-check every ledger item.
Preserve unrelated behavior and do not replace requested behavior with a
mock, proxy, or look-alike implementation.

### D.3 ProgramBench

The ProgramBench medium-mode harness uses a fixed GPT-5.5 high-effort
profile instead of task-adaptive routing. The workflow builds an
independent program from bundled documentation and permitted black-box
probes, validates it against the public reference, and reserves time for
a clean offline rebuild. Listing  shows the stored harness files. This
fixed-profile harness has no routing rubric. The evaluator configures
Codex to load the instruction file and execute the budget hook.
````
